content.title: John Morgan - POLITICO Power List
content.text: The Florida Democratic Party’s fall convention in October was supposed to highlight its top candidates for governor — but it was John Morgan, away from the stage, who stole the show. Morgan, a retinue of allies and relatives in tow, could barely walk a few feet in Disney's Coronado Springs Resort without being asked for a picture or a handshake, or a question about running for governor himself. Indeed, the independently wealthy trial attorney is recognized almost everywhere he goes — and not just because of the nonstop ads for his Morgan & Morgan firm.As an outspoken renegade Democratic donor, the godfather of Florida’s medical marijuana amendment and the force behind a 2020 initiative to boost the state’s minimum wage, Morgan has made himself the center of political gravity in the governor’s race. And after Thanksgiving, Morgan dominated the headlines by announcing on Twitter that if he decided to enter the race, he’d do so only as an independent.“I had a Thanksgiving epiphany. … I am more an independent than a member of a party,” Morgan told Playbook. “What Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump taught us is there’s this vast group of independents out there who are just fed up. They’re not really Democrats and not really Republicans.”Republican Rep. Matt Gaetz, who represents a heavily conservative district in Florida’s Panhandle, said Morgan can’t help but be in the spotlight.“The organizing principle of American politics today is to be interesting. And John Morgan is more interesting than the current candidates for governor by nine furlongs,” Gaetz said.Morgan made it clear he was unimpressed by the current Democrats in the race: former U.S. Rep. Gwen Graham, Orlando businessman Chris King, Tallahassee Mayor Andrew Gillum and Miami Beach Mayor Phil Levine. "I went to the Democratic dinner and listened to blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah,” Morgan said of the October convention forum, which Levine did not attend. “I wasn’t inspired. I didn’t feel passion. I just left.”If Morgan ends up running, it’s likely good news for Republicans, given the nature of Florida’s partisan election system. But the GOP shouldn’t celebrate just yet: Morgan has not switched his party registration, thereby leaving him the option to still enter the Democratic primary next year.“I could do anything. My process right now is to just be done with it. Dial myself way back,” Morgan said when asked about the chance he might still run as a Democrat. “I’m free to be free.” — Marc CaputoMain page photo by Brendan Farrington/AP Photo.
